t: 2729. Check if The Number is Fascinating
o: A 3-digit n is fascinating if concatenating n, 2n, 3n yields a 9-character string containing each digit 1–9 exactly once (no zeros). For n=192 we get 192384576 — a permutation of 123456789. For n=100 we get 100200300, which fails. Since n ≤ 999 the concatenated string always has exactly 9 characters, so we only need to verify it is a permutation of "123456789".
k: Concatenation always has length 9, so just compare against the fixed target "123456789".
Sorting the characters (or counting them) reduces the check to one comparison.
If 2n or 3n exceeds 999 the string still has length 9 but must contain a 0 or repeat, so it fails automatically.

a.i: Build the 9-character string and check whether its sorted form equals "123456789". Any zero or repeated digit breaks the sorted equality.
a.t: O(1) — the string has constant length 9.

a.i: Count occurrences of each character; fascinating iff every digit '1'..'9' appears exactly once and '0' appears zero times.

w: Either approach is instant for these constraints; the sorted-comparison is the most elegant one-liner. Only pitfall: remember zeros are forbidden (the sorted check handles this implicitly). A fun follow-up: precompute all fascinating numbers — there are very few (192, 219, 273, 327...).
